body.head:
DEḤIQ: EXCEPTIONS TO
THE STANDARD PATTERN
body.byline:
E. J. Revell
University of Toronto
body.p:
1. Deḥiq typically occurs in the first letter of a word of
which the first full vowel is stressed, and which follows a word
ending in unstressed segol or qameṣ, where the two are joined
by maqqef or by a conjunctive accent. It does not occur where
the letter in question is waw, 'alef, he, ḥet, or 'ayin, (but it does
occur in resh). Where the unstressed vowel at the end of the
preceding word is followed by 'alef, deḥiq either does not
occur, or is extremely rare, in biblical Hebrew.¹ Consequently, a
pair of words joined by maqqef or a conjunctive accent is
called a standard pair for the occurrence of deḥiq where the
first word ends in unstressed qameṣ or segol which is not
followed by 'alef, and the second begins with a letter other
than waw, 'alef, he, ḥet or 'ayin, and is stressed on its first full
vowel. For purposes of this study, where the first word of a
pair has the postpositive conjunctive accent telisha qeṭanna (so
that its stress position is uncertain), the pair is considered
standard where stress on that word would typically be
body.note:
1. Deḥiq does occur in the Aleppo Codex (A) after
segol followed by 'alef in Prov 23:31. It does not occur here in the
Leningrad Codex (L), but does occur after qameṣ followed by 'alef in
the Aramaic parts of the Bible. See #3.4.
body.p: penultimate, not otherwise. In Exodus 20:3, 4, and the parallels in Deut 5:7, 8, two words which form a standard pair are joined by maqqef in one scheme of accentuation (the “upper”), but in the other (the “lower”) they are joined by a conjunctive accent which marks stress on the first word as final. These pairs also are not considered as “standard” here.As is customary, both sets of accents are shown on the words in L (as in BHS). Conjunctive dagesh does not occur in the second word of these pairs, as is consistent with the lower accentuation.

2. As was shown in the paper I read at the last meeting of this society,Masoretic Studies 6; 95–101. the standard pattern of the occurrence of deḥiq can be described very simply.The following description is based on L. The numbers refer to a list of standard pairs which was created from computer search of the FCAT text (for the use of which I am most grateful), and from a computer-generated list created independently by Richard L. Goerwitz III of Chicago (to whom I offer thanks for his very kind help), and from a manual search (by which a few cases of unusual format or accentuation were added). The list should, then, be nearly, if not quite complete.

2.1 GROUP 1. Deḥiq occurs where the first word in a standard pair ends in unstressed segol, as עֶֽשֶׂה־לּוֹ (Gen 2:18). The first word of the pair is usually an imperfect verb form from a root IIIh, as in the example. In a few cases it is a participle or other noun from such a root, or a pronoun (זֶה, אֵלֶּה). There are 17 exceptions in 277 cases (6%).

2.2 GROUP 2. Deḥiq occurs where the first word in a standared pair ends in unstressed qameṣ and (i) never had final stress, as עָשִׂיתָ זֹּאת (Gen 3:14), or (ii) has its typical final stress nullified by maqqef or nesiga, but has typical final stress in MT only due to a shift which occurred relatively recently in the history of the language, as אֶעֱשֶׂה־לָּךְ (Jer 5:5), and 2m.s perfect forms with waw consecutive (on which see #8.1). The first word is usually a verb form: 2m.s or 3f.s perfect, modal with affixed qameṣ he (1st person imperfect, or m.s imperative, including

הָבָה) or f.pl imperfect. It may also be a noun form with affixed qameṣ he “directional,” or with the ending -’ātāh (GK #90.g), a verb, noun, or preposition with a pronominal suffix, or a pronoun or other particle (חָלִילָה, לָמָּה, מְא֫וּמָה, הֵמָּה). In group 2 overall, there are 41 exceptions in 548 cases (7%). Of these exceptions, 17 occur in group 2.ii, where they form 9% of the total.

2.3 GROUP 3. Deḥiq does not occur where the first word ends in qameṣ which is unstressed through maqqef or nesiga, but (apart from such special features of the reading tradition) has always been typically stressed in recent history of the language, as תִּקְרָה לָּךְ (Gen 4:6). The first word is most commonly a 3m.s perfect verb form from a root IIIh, as in the example. It may also be a noun with the typical feminine ending qameṣ he (including the unusual forms אָנִ֫יָּה Ps 120:5, לְהָקָ֫מָה Dan 2:46). In Dan 2:29 it is the interrogative מָה; in Amos 1:11 it is שָׁמְרָה, the last syllable of which represents the 3f.s pronoun. There is one exception in 189 cases (1%).
body.head: Regular Exceptions
body.p: 3. When deḥiq is described in this way, it becomes clear that its use is much more regular than is generally supposed. Moreover, the description above gives gross figures for exceptions. In some cases, exceptions to the rule given include most, or all, members of a group which is defined by phonological or morphological features, and so can be considered as regular features of the overall pattern.

3.1 Deḥiq does not occur in the second word of a standard pair where this is a noun (stressed on its first syllable) with a prefixed preposition (לְ֫ or בְּ֫). It is noteworthy that all thirteen pairs showing this exception occur in group 2. In group 1, deḥiq does occur in initial prepositional lamed even where followed by a noun in יִהְיֶה־לְּעָם (Gen 48:19). It is noteworthy that in standard pairs of which the first letter of the second word is followed by shewa, but does not represent a preposition, the word is a noun with initial mem or shin.

3.2 Dehiq does not occur in L in eight of nine cases in which the second word of a standard pair has dagesh in its second letter (שָׁמָּה, מִזֶּה). In L, dagesh following מַה is omitted from mem and shin and some other letters under the same conditions, as pointed out by Dotan.See A. Dotan, "Deviation in Gemination in the Tiberian Vocalization," in Estudios Masoreticos (Textos y Estudios vol. 33, ed. E. Fernández-Tejero, Madrid, 1983, p. 67). Dehiq occurs in such words in A, and in the Cairo Codex (C).

3.3 Dehiq does not occur where the first word of a standard pair is a feminine plural imperfect or imperative form in which the stressed penultimate vowel is segol, (except where the following nun has dagesh as in Mic. 7:10 (תִּרְאֶינָה בָּהּ).

3.4 In the Aramaic sections of L, dehiq occurs where the first word of a standard pair ends in unstressed qameṣ followed by 'alef where this word is a first person plural perfect verb (as אֲמַרְנָה לְהֹם Ezra 5:4, 9, also 5:10). It does not where the first word in the pair is the negative particle לָא (Dan 3:12, 27, 6:14, 25), or a noun in the determined state (as וְעִבְיָתָא דָה Ezra 5:8, also Dan 4:9, 18, 7:8) with the exception of דִּלָא חֲפָא (Dan 4:25).
body.head: Irregular Exceptions
body.p: 4. If these "regular exceptions" are treated as features of standard usage, the largest group of cases in which dehiq is expected but does not appear belong to division (ii) of group 2: pairs in which the first word is a verb form (or, in two cases, Gen 24:42, Ps 109:27, a noun with a 2m.s pronominal suffix) which shows final stress in MT (in its typical medial form) as the result of a shift from penultimate stress which occurred relatively recently. It is not surprising to find that, in a phenomenon which is conditioned by stress position, exceptions occur where this has recently changed.
4.1 In group 2.ii, dehiq almost always occurs where the second word of the pair has the form CV or CVC. This occurs
with a noun in 17 cases, a preposition with a pronominal suffix in 92 cases, an adverb in 4 cases, and with the particle נָא in 34 cases. Three exceptions occur.

4.1.1 Where the second word of the pair is a preposition with a pronominal suffix in Exod 21:4 נָתַן־לּוֹ - the same pair shows dehiq in Gen 21:3 and elsewhere; Jer 20:10 וְנִוָּכְלָה לּוֹ - there is no exact parallel to this, but a similar pair occurs in Ps 83:13 נִירְשָׁה לָּנוּ (also 1 Kgs 17:17, Jer 5:5); Job 5:23 הָשְׁלְמָה־לָּךְ. The closest parallel structure in L is שָׁחֲבָה־לָּהּ (Ps 122:3). These cases appear to be anomalies. British Library MS Or. 4445 (B) agrees with L in Exod 21:4, as do A and C in Jer 20:10. However A shows dagesh in the case in Job 5:23, so its absence in L may be due to error.

4.1.2 Dehiq does not occur where the second word is the noun רָע in אֹהֵב־רָע Prov 21:10 (also Prov 20:22). There are no cases in this group in which dehiq occurs in resh, so possibly its absence in these cases is conditioned by the phonological characteristics of this consonant.

4.2 Where the first word is a verb, and the second is a preposition with a suffix composing a word of form CVCV, dehiq occurs in all nine cases, as in נִירְשָׁה־לָּנוּ (Ps 83:13). Where the second word is a noun of form CVCV or CVCVC, dehiq occurs in only five of nine cases.

4.2.1 Dehiq occurs where the noun is the object of the preceding verb, which is preceded by its subject or a modifier. The clause is marked with revia' mugrash and silluq, and forms the second and final half of a verse of poetry, as Job 5:16 וְעוֹלָתָה קָפְצָה פִּיהָ (also Ps 26:10, 107:42, Prov 31:16), or is marked with dehi and atnaḥ following 'ole we-yored, and forms the first division of the second part of the verse (Prov 30:16). Dehiq also occurs in נֶעֶמְדָה יָחַד (which forms a clause ending the first half of Isa 50:8), the only case with a verb of this form.

4.2.2 Dehiq does not occur in subject - verb - object structures which begin the verse in Ps 84:4, Job 24:15 (the latter is not a complete clause). It does not occur in accentual units of the type described in #4.2.1 where the first word of the pair is preceded by another verb (not by a subject or modifier) in Prov 30:20 אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִּיהָ, nor in the similar structure which

begins Isa 56:12, nor in אָמְלְלָה־נָפֶשׁ (Isa 24:7), the second of two two-word clauses of structure verb - subject. That is, the situations in which dehiq does occur differ from those in which it does not occur. The specific differences could produce prosodic features which could condition its use.

4.3 Dehiq also does not occur in group 2.ii where the second word has shewa under its first letter; the word is a preposition with a pronominal suffix in אָחָזְךָ־לָּךְ (1 Kgs 21:2, 6), a noun in תִּגָּה־נִי (Prov 23:26). There are no cases of this sort in which dehiq does occur.

4.4 It seems clear, then, that, in group 2.ii, the occurrence of dehiq is conditioned by the form of the second word, and by its relationship to the first. It appears that the occurrence of dehiq is inhibited where the second word is “long” in that the stressed vowel is followed by another vowel (#4.2), or preceded by a consonant with shewa (#4.3). It also seems probable that it is inhibited where the initial consonant of the second word is resh. On the question of relationship, the fact that a word of form CVCV always shows dehiq where it is a preposition with a pronominal suffix, but not always where it is a noun, suggests that syntactic/semantic relationship of the sort which affects the occurrence of nesiga was significant here also. It is assumed (as with nesiga) that it was prosodic patterns reflecting these relationships which actually conditioned the use of dehiq.This suggests, then, that the occurrence of dehiq is determined by a combination of phonotactic and prosodic features, as has been shown to be the case for other types of sound variation.The
body.note: 6. See E. J. Revell, Nesiga in Tiberian Hebrew (Textos y Estudios vol. 39), Madrid 1987, #2.53. The fact that the accentuation does not indicate the conditions under which dehiq (or nesiga) must occur, but only those under which it may occur, shows that the accentuation does not exactly represent the prosodic features which conditioned these phenomena, as argued in #1.15 there.
7. Specifically nesiga, and the stressing of perfect verb forms with waw consecutive, and of verb forms with vocalic affix from hollow or geminate roots. See the remarks in my article “Stress
body.p: effect of any particular feature, such as the prosodic pattern reflecting the relationship between the two words, or the presence of resh or a consonant with shewa at the beginning of the second, is dependent on the other features with which it is combined. No feature conditions such variation independently, as is already indicated, for dehiq, by the fact that the standard pair is characterized by a combination of features, not by one alone.
5. The remaining cases in which dehiq fails to occur where expected in a standard pair can be treated together. Most occur in category 1.

5.1 Dehiq fails to occur in יִהְיֶה־קֹּדֶשׁ (Lev 27:33), but does occur here in B, as it does in L in the same pair in Lev 27:9, 10, 32, (and in 17 other cases in a pair composed of a verb followed by a segolate noun). It fails to occur in הַמְּחַיֶּה־לָּנוּ (1 Kgs 20:25), but occurs in לָּךְ in 14 other cases. Dehiq also fails to occur in חָרְעָה־רֶמֶף (Jer 22:22). Dehiq does occur in fourteen other cases in nouns of form CVC, including nouns with initial resh in Prov 11:21, Job 39:9. There are no other examples in which the vowel is followed by patah furtive, but it seems probable that both this and the other cases treated in this paragraph are isolated anomalies.

5.2 Where the first word of a standard pair is the pronoun אֵלֶּה, dehiq occurs in five cases in which the second word of the pair is a preposition with a pronominal suffix, as מִי־אֵלֶּה לָּךְ (Gen 33:5, and similar structures 2 Sam 16:2, Ezek 24:19, 37:18), and אֲשֶׁר־אֵלֶּה לּוֹ (Gen 38:25). Dehiq does not occur in the pair וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמֹות (Gen 46:8, Exod 6:16. B agrees with L). There is no other example of a standard pair in which (as here) the second word is a construct noun. The first word in such cases (i.e. a word preceding a construct noun) typically has a disjunctive accent (as in the other cases of ואלה שמות) showing that the second word of the pair is more closely related to
Position in Hebrew Verb Forms with Vocalic Affix” JSS 32 (1987), 263 (#21).
body.head: 92 E. J. Revell
body.p: what follows than to what precedes (i.e. the first word). Presumably this relatively weak relationship of the two words in the pair וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹת prevented the development of dehiq, despite the fact that the words were joined by a conjunctive accent, as also occurs with nesiga. The other two cases in which dehiq fails to occur in a standard pair of which the first word is אֵלֶּה are אֲנַחְנוּ אֵלֶּה פֹּה (Deut 5:3), and שְׁחַרְיָאֵלֶּה רָבַע (Isa 47:9). In both cases, the two words forming the pair belong to different constituents of the clause. It seems possible that here, too, the prosodic features reflecting the syntactic/semantic relationship of the words forming the pair inhibited the development of dehiq. Again parallels can be found in the occurrence of nesiga.8. For the failure of nesiga to occur in a word followed by a construct phrase, see Revell Nesiga #2.3. For its typical failure to occur where the two words in the pair have no direct grammatical relationship, see #7.7 there.

5.3 There is no close parallel to בְּדֶרֶךְ עֵדְוֹתֶיךָ שַׂשְׂתִּי (Ps 119:14). There are cases in this group (2.i) in which dehiq is shown in a pair of which the first word ends a phrase (as Deut 23:6, 2 Sam 9:10, Ps 61:5), and in pairs in which the first word modifies a following verb (as Ezek 40:4, 44:5), but no other example shows both features. It seems possible that the prosodic features reflecting this pair of relationships also inhibited the development of dehiq.

5.4 Dehiq fails to occur in L in Gen 23:9, יִתְנֶנָּה לִּי - dagesh occurs in closely similar pairs in 1 Sam 18:21, 21:10. Dehiq also fails to occur in וּבְאָזְנֶיךָ תִּשְׁמָע (Ezek 3:10), where it occurs in A and C, as in all three MSS in the same pair in Ezek 40:4, 44:5. Consequently this case appears to be due to error in L. That in Gen 23:9 may also be due to error, but B is not available for comparison.
5.5 The exceptions to the standard pattern of the occurrence of dehiq treated in this section, then, include a
body.head: Dehiq: Exceptions to Standard Pattern 93
body.p: number of isolated anomalies which may arise from error.9. It seems safe to assume that such anomalies in L are errors where one of the other MSS closely associated with ben Asher (A, B, or C) shows the expected pattern. However, these MSS support L in some anomalies (as in Exod 21:4, Jer 20:10, see #4.1.1) and each shows anomalies of its own (as the use of dehiq after alef in A in Prov 23:31, and its absence in B in Lev 15:26), so it cannot be certain that any anomaly is foreign to the tradition. Other MSS in the fairly wide range of codices and Genizah fragments which I have now checked all show some variation from L which cannot be supported from A, B, or C, so it cannot be certain that any of these represents the true tradition, even where it shows the expected pattern where L does not. They also include a number of cases which suggest quite strongly that its occurrence was conditioned by the prosodic features representing the syntactic/semantic relationships of the words in question.

list.item:
6. Dehiq occurs in two cases in the second word of a standard pair where it is contrary to the standard pattern.
6.1 The use of dehiq in יָרְדָה פְּלָאִים (Lam 1:16) contrasts with its absence in מָשְׁלָה לוֹ (Isa 40:10), קָצְרָה יָדוֹ (Isa 59:19). Features of Tiberian pointing strongly suggest that a participle was treated as a perfect verb (with consequent minor adjustment of stress position and vowel pattern) if both its morphological features and its syntactic/semantic context would allow this.10. See E. J. Revell “‘Obed (Deut 26:5) and the Function of the Participle in MT.” Sefarad 48 (1988), 197–205. The participle in Lam 1:16 could have been treated in this way (it is followed by perfect verbs) while those in Isa 40:10, and Isa 59:19, which stand in a present/future context, were not. The failure to use dehiq in these two cases is expected after nouns (group 3).11. The treatment of other forms which could be classed either as verbs or as nouns is consistent with this. חָתְנָה (1 Kgs 17:17, Ezek 14:22) and וְחָתְוָה (2 Kgs 25:30 = Jer 52:34) are followed by dehiq, reflecting the fact that they were understood as perfect verb forms. The time value of חָתְנָה in Ezek 14:22 may seem questionable, but it

body.p: that it is not clear that יָרְדָה in Lam 1:16 was regarded as a perfect verb,It is represented by an aorist in the Greek translation, but by a participle in Jerome’s and the Targum (ולנחי). and that the discussion in #4.2 leaves it uncertain as to whether deḥiq should be expected even if it were so regarded. The explanation offered here is, then, questionable, but the only alternative is to regard the form as anomalous.
6.2 In וְעָנְתָה שָׁמָּה (Hos 2:17), the use of deḥiq is atypical of L (see #3.2) although not of A and C. This may simply represent error or inconsistency in the naqdan of L.
body.head: Other Situations
body.p: 7. Dagesh occurs in a number of cases where the second word of a pair which is otherwise standard is not stressed on its first full vowel. The following groupings suggest that this phenomenon also is phonologically conditioned.
7.1 Dagesh occurs in word-initial lamed in the neighborhood of lamed or resh.
body.note: was translated as past in the Targum, the Greek, and Jerome. The context in which the other three forms occur is clearly past. In Dan 10:17, וְנִשְׁמָה occurs in a present/future context. (Note the preceding מעתה לא יעמד. The form is translated as past in the Greek, but as present by Jerome, and with an imperfect form in Saadya’s Arabic). Deḥiq is not used in this case in Daniel, reflecting the fact that it was treated as a noun – i.e. as a participle with present/future value where used predicatively.
body.p: Ps 19:3 should also probably be included here, since, although the words form a standard pair in category 2.2.1, the use of deḥiq is anomalous according to #3.1. Dagesh also occurs in this environment after stressed segol in Hab 2:6 הַמַּרְבֶּה לּא־לוֹ, and in לֹא where followed by לוֹ elsewhere (Gen 38:9, Hab 1:6, Prov 26:17). It also seems possible that the use of dagesh in וַיֹּאמְרוּ לּוֹ (Gen 19:2, 1 Sam 8:19) is a related phenomenon,The use of dagesh here might be merely diacritical, distinguishing לא from לוֹ. However, ויאמרו לו regularly shows nesiga, and so is distinguished from ויאמרו לא even without the dagesh. It is interesting to note that in Jud 18:19, Est 6:13, where the accent on the verb is the typically postpositive telisha qeṭanna, L repeats it on the stressed syllable to mark the retraction of the stress. (The statement of S. Baer in "De primarum vocabulorum literarum dagessatione" [Liber Proverbiorum edd. S. Baer and F. Delitzsch, Lipsiae 1880, vii–xv], #7, p. xiv, that in these two cases [out of all the cases of ויאמרו לו] the lamed has dagesh, probably does not reflect a genuine tradition. I have found no sources which show dagesh in Jud 18:19. That a few do in Est 6:13 – including the Venice ed. of 1624–5 – may well be due to confusion. Baer’s statement [#8 there, p. xv] that there is dagesh in the lamed of לא in לו לא in Deut 32:5 probably arises from similar confusion. There is no dagesh in L, as is to be expected if this dagesh represents a conditioned phonological variation related to deḥiq, as לו here has a disjunctive accent). possibly also that in מֹשֶׁה לּאמֹר (Exod 6:10 etc.).
7.2 Dagesh occurs in word-initial mem
Dagesh also occurs after זֶה in וְזֶה־פִּרְיָהּ (Num 13:27) as it does wherever the following word is stressed on its first syllable. Elsewhere, the first letter of the following word does
body.head: E. J. Revell
body.p: not show dagesh. The word is יִהְיֶה in Num 18:9, 34:6, 9, Jos 15:4, and a perfect qal form, also beginning with yod, in Ps 56:10, 104:26. Cf. the fact that dagesh fails to occur in yod following מַה (but consistently only where the yod is followed by shewa). Dagesh does not occur after פֶּה in the closest parallels (פֶּה־לָהֶם Ps 115:5, 135:16), but since the situation differs from that described in #7.1, it is not clear that it should be expected here.

נָא as second word in a standard pair regularly shows dehiq. It also shows dagesh after stressed qames or segol (i) where נָא is not stressed, after אָנָּסָה (Jud 6:39) and הִנָּה (Gen 19:2),נָא following הִנֵּה is elsewhere stressed. The two are usually joined by maqqef, and הִנֵּה has ṣere, as it does in Jud 19:9, where both words have conjunctive accents. and (ii) where נָא is stressed, after אִמְלָּטָה (Gen 19:20), הוֹשִׁיעָה and הַצְלִיחָה (Ps 118:25). It appears that there are no parallels to situation (i) in which the nun is rafe, that is, dagesh always occurs in unstressed נָא. There are parallels to situation (ii) in which dagesh is not marked in stressed נָא, as after אֶבְרָחָה (2 Sam 17:1), שִׁלְחָה (2 Kgs 4:22). Of the cases where dagesh is shown, that in Gen 19.20 is the only case in which nesiga does not occur in a verb followed by נָא where the two form a typical pair for that phenomenon, and final stress is anomalous in the two cases in Ps 118:25.For notes on these cases in relation to nesiga, see Revell, Nesiga, #1.14, #2.12 (v). Consequently it seems very likely that, in these three cases, dehiq arose in a form of tradition in which the common patterns of nesiga and word stress were followed.
body.head: Dehiq: Exceptions to Standard Pattern

list.head: 7.5 Dagesh occurs in a word-initial sibilant
7.6 Dagesh occurs in a word-initial begad-kefat letter

body.p: 8. Dagesh may, then, occur in almost any letter under conditions related to those typical for dehiq, but occurs most commonly in lamed, mem, and nun. As is well known, these
body.note: 16. Some cases which could have been included here were omitted because they also belong to the category שתי אותיות רצופות, which is, like דחיק and אתי מרחיק one of the מבטלים phenomena which block the conditions which induce the fricative (rafe) realization of the בגד כפ"ת. Examples are וְהִטַפְתָּ בְּמֵיכָם (Jer 44:25, cf. Ezra 8:17), אֱמוּנָתְךָ כְּפִי (Ps 89.2). Descriptions of the conditioning of this phenomenon vary. For an early example see Ilan Eldar, "חוק אריה ובוגנכפ"ת", Hebrew Union College Annual 55 (1984), p. יב. Since the use of the dagesh here is not conditioned by the form of the preceding word, there is no reason to connect it with dehiq.
body.head: E. J. Revell
body.p: letters show other unusual uses of dagesh in some non-standard forms of pointing. As remarked in #7.1 and note 16, some other cases of "deḥiq-related" dagesh seem equally to be related to uses of dagesh which bear no obvious relation to deḥiq. This suggests that what is here called deḥiq is merely the most common case of phenomenon which occurred in a considerably wider context. A great deal of work is needed before this wider context can be fully understood. More work is needed even to establish whether the use of dagesh in the cases listed in ##7.1-3 is conditioned in some way, or is merely sporadic.The ga‘ya which (in Baer's opinion, op. cit., #6.d) governs the use of deḥiq in such cases is not always admissible in the examples, and is not always marked in L where it could be. There is, however, no doubt about the regularity of the standard form of deḥiq. The cases which are certainly anomalies (the seven pairs designated as anomalous in ##5.1, 4, 6.1, 2) form less than 1% of the total. Whether these arose in the process of transmission, or represent a feature of the tradition which is not understood, they form a proportion far too small to affect the conclusion that the standard form of deḥiq arises from automatic phonological conditioning.

list.item: 9. The necessity of mentioning shifts in stress position in the definition of group 2.ii of the standard pattern shows that deḥiq has implications for the history of the language. These cannot be explored in full, but their importance can be illustrated by one point. Deḥiq occurs consistently after 2m.s perfect forms with waw consecutive where these have maqqef, or a conjunctive accent with penultimate stress, just as it does after the same forms with no prefixed conjunction. That is, in the matter of deḥiq, waw consecutive perfect forms act as members of group 2.ii. In the other forms in this sub-group, the penultimate syllable, which was open with a short vowel, was stressed until a period relatively recent in the history of the Tiberian tradition, as is well known. The fact that 2m.s perfect forms with waw consecutive act in the same way seems to me

body.head: Deḥiq: Exceptions to Standard Pattern
body.p: to confirm the conclusion that the shift of stress to the final vowel from the long (closed) penultimate syllable of such forms is a late development in biblical Hebrew, occurring after the shift of stress to a final vowel from a short penultimate syllable.See JAOS 104 (1984), 440 (#9). Note also that the variation in stress position in these forms appears to be conditioned in the same way as is nesiga and other late variation in stress position. See n. 7 above. In Matres Lectionis in Early Hebrew Epigraphs (American Schools of Oriental Research Monographs 2, Cambridge, Mass., 1980, 31–2) Ziony Zevit suggests that orthographic features of the pre-exilic inscriptions reflect the final stressing of 2m.s perfect forms with waw consecutive in those times. His argument is reasonable, but the evidence can be explained in other ways (see, e.g., for two of the forms cited, F. M. Cross and D. N. Freedman, Early Hebrew Orthography [American Oriental Series 36] New Haven 1952, p. 53, #54.
